source.title: Accelerating Adversarial Suffix Optimization via Continuous Relaxation and Activation-Guided Objectives
source.authors: Ege Çakar; Hannah Guan; Kayden Kehe

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates a refusal-direction ablation baseline using the direction and ablation approach attributed to Arditi et al., and reports harmful-prompt ASR. It also tests suffix attacks whose objective minimizes projections onto that direction.
record.gate_note: The selected layer and position for the refusal direction were chosen using ablation scores on training splits; those selection values are not recorded as results. Soft-GCG, Gemma results, and the ordinary GCG comparator do not target the refusal direction and are not rows. The study does not report achieved projection values for the learned suffixes.
record.test_reason: The study reports harmful-prompt ASR for the Arditi et al. difference-in-means direction ablation on Llama-2-7b-chat, with a no-intervention baseline, which bears on V1. It also optimizes input suffixes to suppress that direction and reports their jailbreak success, which bears on V3. The direction is used as an attack tool, but the ablation and suppression outcomes are reported results.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The abstract states more strongly that safety representations are distributed across the forward pass rather than localized. The authors also claim their results confirm Arditi et al.'s refusal-feature account. Only the results section hedges that broader objectives may just give richer gradients. Separately, they report that larger Gemma3 models resist Soft-GCG; this is speculatively linked to higher-rank refusal but not tested.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a precomputed difference-in-means refusal direction and evaluates a refusal-direction ablation baseline, but the main contribution is suffix optimization with activation-based objectives rather than the original ablation-and-addition tests. No addition-to-harmless-prompts or capability-preservation test is reported.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported ASR depends strongly on the evaluator: substring ASR is much higher than LlamaGuard 4 and HarmBench ASR for the direction-targeting suffixes and the ablation condition. Among suffix objectives, All has the highest substring ASR.

fits_no_version.finding: The All-layers/positions suppression objective gets higher substring ASR than the Single layer-position objective (0.91 vs 0.84). Authors read this as refusal being distributed, but concede richer gradient signal is an alternative explanation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-direction suppression is more effective as an attack objective when applied across all layers and positions than at a single site.

record.peer_reviewed: To appear at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Representational Alignment (Re-Align)
record.problems: Only one chat model is used for Activation-Guided GCG. The authors note substring matching can yield false positives and false negatives; their activation-guided table has sharply different ASR across evaluation methods. No uncertainty estimates are reported for those results, and the study does not test harmless-request refusal or retained general capability.
record.rows_left_out: Section 4.2 and Table 2 report Soft-GCG and Gemma suffix-attack results, but those methods do not target the refusal direction. The GCG comparator in Table 1 is an output-targeting suffix attack rather than a direction-targeting intervention. These results were therefore not catalogued as rows for the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts. Preservation of other capabilities. Models other than Llama-2-7b-chat. The exact ablation scope (layers and positions) is not stated.

Whether existing attacks such as GCG work by suppressing the direction. Whether the learned suffixes actually lower the projection (no projection values reported). Training against ablation for robustness.

missing.what: Output-targeting GCG comparator at 200 steps: substring 0.76, LlamaGuard 0.00, HarmBench 0.00. This is needed to judge whether direction-targeting adds anything over a standard attack for V3.

record.verdict_notes: The study uses a single model. Substring ASR diverges sharply from the classifier judges, and the 0.39 substring baseline indicates substring false positives, so the substring-based supports should be read cautiously. No uncertainty is reported for Table 1. The Gemma/Soft-GCG results do not use the refusal direction and are correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports harmful-prompt outcomes for a refusal-direction ablation baseline, but does not test adding the direction on harmless prompts or whether other abilities are preserved. The ablation scope is not specified in enough detail here to establish that every layer and position was ablated.

Tests suffix optimization with objectives targeting the refusal direction, but does not measure whether the resulting suffixes suppress the direction. Training against ablation to add robustness is not tested.
No test of affine refusal regions, cones, or multiple refusal directions. Comparing objective scopes is not a direct test of those representational alternatives.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No transfer test of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or stages.

relation.reason: Reports its own ablation results against a no-intervention baseline (V1). It also reports the jailbreak rates of suffixes optimised to suppress the direction (V3).

tranche.reason: The study runs the Arditi precomputed difference-in-means direction ablation on Llama-2-7b-chat, one of the original's models. It scores the outputs by refusal substrings plus guard classifiers, close to the original's method and measure. The suffix objectives add a V3 test.

source_check.notes: The pack listed four verdicts with no [lN] ids, so label_id is left blank; they are returned in pack order (V1 supports, V1 limits_scope, V3 supports, V3 limits_scope). Table 1 gives no n or uncertainty, and the Table 1 GCG comparator (0.76/0.00/0.00) has no row. The abstract says larger models resist activation-based attacks, but Activation-Guided GCG ran only on Llama-2-7b-chat; the Gemma3 results are Soft-GCG with substring ASR only. Judge versions are inconsistent: the table says LlamaGuard 4, but the cited reference is Llama Guard 2.
